extraction.name: LAMBADA
extraction.description: A dataset to evaluate the capabilities of computational models for text understanding by means of a word prediction task requiring a broad discourse context.
extraction.creator: Denis Paperno, Germán Kruszewski, Angeliki Lazaridou, Quan Ngoc Pham, Raffaella Bernardi, Sandro Pezzelle, Marco Baroni, Gemma Boleda, Raquel Fernández
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Passages were extracted from the Book Corpus, filtered by language models to remove easy cases, and then evaluated by human subjects through crowdsourcing to ensure the target word could be guessed from the broad context but not the local context.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Manual Human Curator
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The Book Corpus, which contains unpublished novels.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The corpus underwent duplicate removal and filtering of potentially offensive material using a stop word list. Passages were then filtered using four language models to exclude those that were relatively easy (target word probability > 0.00175). Finally, a random sample of the remaining passages was evaluated by human subjects in a three-step crowdsourcing pipeline, where passages were discarded if subjects could not guess the target word from the broad context or if they could guess it from the local sentence context alone.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Duplicate removal, filtering out potentially offensive material with a stop word list, and filtering out passages whose target word had a probability >= 0.00175 according to four language models.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Human subjects guessed the target word based on the whole passage (two consecutive subjects had to guess right), and then up to 10 subjects tried to guess it based on the target sentence only (none could guess it for the passage to be included).
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: A strict perfect-match approach was used, requiring two consecutive subjects to exactly match the missing word, and ensuring no subject out of ten could provide it based on local context only.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: Up to 12 human guesses per passage (2 for the whole passage, up to 10 for the target sentence only).
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: Four language models: a pre-trained recurrent neural network (RNN), a standard 4-gram model, a RNN, and a feed-forward model.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: Proper nouns are hugely over-represented in LAMBADA, while other categories are under-represented compared to the POS distribution in the input.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Standard language models are bound to fail on it by design because the dataset was explicitly filtered to remove passages where simple language models succeed.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Evaluating the capabilities of computational models for text understanding by means of a word prediction task requiring broad discourse context.

name.evidence: We introduce LAMBADA, a dataset to evaluate the capabilities of computational models for text understanding by means of a word prediction task.

description.evidence: LAMBADA is a collection of narrative passages sharing the characteristic that human subjects are able to guess their last word if they are exposed to the whole passage, but not if they only see the last sentence preceding the target word.

url.evidence: The development set of LAMBADA, along with the training corpus, can be downloaded at http://clic.cimec.unitn.it/lambada/ .

inLanguage.evidence: LAMBADA proposes a word prediction task where the target item is difficult to guess (for English speakers) when only the sentence in which it appears is available

rai:dataCollection.evidence: The LAMBADA data come from the Book Corpus... We filtered out passages that are relatively easy for standard language models... A random sample of the remaining passages were then evaluated by human subjects through the CrowdFlower crowdsourcing service in three steps.

rai:dataCollectionType.evidence: The LAMBADA data come from the Book Corpus (Zhu et al., 2015)... A random sample of the remaining passages were then evaluated by human subjects through the CrowdFlower crowdsourcing service

rai:dataCollectionRawData.evidence: The LAMBADA data come from the Book Corpus (Zhu et al., 2015). The fact that it contains unpublished novels minimizes the potential usefulness of general world knowledge and extemal resources for the task

rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol.evidence: The corpus, after duplicate removal and filtering out of potentially offensive material with a stop word list... Any passage whose target word had probability >= 0.00175 according to any of the language models was excluded.

rai:dataAnnotationProtocol.evidence: 1. one human subject guessed the target word based on the whole passage... 2. a second subject guessed the target word based on the whole passage... 3. more subjects tried to guess the target word based on the target sentence only, until the word was guessed or the number of unsuccessful guesses reached 10; if no subject was able to guess the target word, the passage was added to the LAMBADA dataset.

rai:dataAnnotationPlatform.evidence: A random sample of the remaining passages were then evaluated by human subjects through the CrowdFlower crowdsourcing service

rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis.evidence: Note that the criteria for passage inclusion were very strict: We required two consecutive subjects to exactly match the missing word, and we made sure that no subject (out of ten) was able to provide it based on local context only, even when given 3 guesses.

rai:annotationsPerItem.evidence: 1. one human subject guessed... 2. a second subject guessed... 3. more subjects tried to guess the target word based on the target sentence only, until the word was guessed or the number of unsuccessful guesses reached 10

rai:machineAnnotationTools.evidence: We used a combination of four language models, chosen by availability and/or ease of training: a pre-trained recurrent neural network (RNN) (Mikolov et al., 2011) and three models trained on the Book Corpus (a standard 4-gram model, a RNN and a feed-forward model...)

rai:dataBiases.evidence: Figure 2(b) shows that most target words in LAMBADA are proper nouns (48%), followed by common nouns (37%) and, at a distance, verbs (7.7%). In fact, proper nouns are hugely overrepresented in LAMBADA, while the other categories are under-represented, compared to the POS distribution in the input.

rai:dataLimitations.evidence: We also note that, because of the way we have constructed LAMBADA, standard language models are bound to fail on it by design: one of our first filters (see Section 3.1) was to choose passages where a number of simple language models were failing to predict the upcoming word.

rai:dataUseCases.evidence: We introduce LAMBADA, a dataset to evaluate the capabilities of computational models for text understanding by means of a word prediction task.
